title: Lecture 12 — counters and sequence design
summary: Trace synchronous counter controls, build a chosen modulus, and turn an arbitrary sequence into next-state equations.
body:
A counter is a finite-state machine whose state usually doubles as its output. Start by separating ripple counting from a shared-clock design. Then trace reset, parallel load, count enable and hold as distinct operations; a changing load input is not itself a clock edge.

For a shortened counting cycle, decide which state is the last visible state and which value the following edge must load. That decision prevents the common off-by-one modulus error. Cascaded synchronous stages share the clock and use a carry condition to enable the upper stage.

Next remove the assumption that the sequence is numerical. Write every present-to-next transition, derive one D equation per state bit and verify all physical codes. The original examples practise a five-state counting interval and a three-state arbitrary cycle, without supplying an assigned lab circuit. Use the existing mux visual to review load selection and the parity machine to practise predicting before clocking.
